_info.comment: EIP-658: what a transaction receipt's FIRST FIELD is. Before Atlantis it is a 32-byte intermediate post-state root, so a receipt cannot say whether its transaction succeeded. From Atlantis it is a status code -- 1 for success, 0 for failure -- and the outcome becomes legible. The encoded receipt is `rlp([postStateOrStatus, cumulativeGasUsed, logsBloom, logs])` either way, so the change is confined to that one field and to everything derived from it: the receipt's RLP, and the RECEIPTS ROOT a block header carries. Vectors come in PAIRS -- the same execution at 8,771,999 and at 8,772,000 -- because only the pair shows that nothing but the encoding moved.
_info.whyThisIsBlockLevelAndNotAStateFixture: A state fixture's post entry carries a post-state root, a logs hash and the signed transaction, and none of those reaches a receipt. Adding a field for one would invent format no reader reads. This is the observable that was recorded as unreachable when the rule ledger closed, and it is the last activation in this chain's mainnet configuration that nothing else asserts.
_info.oracle: Computed from the RLP and Merkle-Patricia rules, not read back from any client. The implementation was calibrated before emitting anything, against three things it could not coincidentally satisfy: the published empty-trie root 56e81f171bcc55a6ff8345e692c0f86e5b48e01b996cadc001622fb5e363b421, published RLP vectors, and -- decisively -- the receipts roots of REAL MAINNET BLOCKS on both sides of the activation, reproduced exactly from their receipts. The logs-bloom derivation was checked the same way against three real receipts carrying logs. See observedMainnet. A FOURTH, fully independent confirmation arrived from the archive itself: multi-geth's own cmd/evm README publishes the transition-tool output for a single successful transaction -- root "0x", status "0x1", cumulativeGasUsed "0x5208", empty bloom, logs null -- and states its receiptRoot as 056b23fbba480696b65fe5a59b8f2148a1299103c4f57df839233af2cf4ca2d2. That is byte-for-byte the root this fixture's boundary_post_one_successful_transaction vector carries. It was written by a client in this chain's own lineage, years before this fixture, and it neither knows nor could have been influenced by anything here. See upstreamPublishedRoot.
_info.oracle-version: derived from EIP-658 and the yellow paper's receipt encoding; grounded against mainnet 2026-08-25
_info.syntheticValues: Post-state roots in the vectors are SYNTHETIC and deterministically derived as keccak256('fukuii-tests synthetic post-state root: ' + tag). They are not real roots and are not meant to be: the rule under test is which FIELD a receipt carries, not what a particular state root is. Any 32-byte value exercises it identically. The addresses and topics are likewise obviously synthetic.
_info.howAHarnessReadsThis: For each vector, build the receipts described, encode each as `rlp([firstField, cumulativeGasUsed, logsBloom, logs])`, and compare against `encodedReceipts`; then insert them into a trie keyed by the RLP-encoded transaction index and compare the root against `receiptsRoot`. `receiptCarriesStatus` is the rule flag: it is what a schedule must resolve to at that height, and it is stated so a harness can check its own resolution rather than infer it from the answer.

upstreamPublishedRoot.forReceipts: one receipt: root "0x" (empty -- the post-EIP-658 form), status "0x1", cumulativeGasUsed "0x5208", empty logsBloom, logs null
upstreamPublishedRoot.whyThisCounts: It is an independently-authored value from a DIFFERENT implementation in this chain's lineage, published in its own documentation rather than derived here. The three prior calibrations proved this implementation reproduces mainnet; this one proves the exact vector the fixture ships was already the right answer according to a client that is not the one under certification.
upstreamPublishedRoot.whyOnlyThisSide: That README documents a post-Byzantium transition tool, so it publishes only the status form. Nothing in the archive publishes a worked pre-EIP-658 receipts root, which is why the pre-activation side rests on real mainnet block 8,771,998 instead -- a stronger grounding, not a weaker one, because it is the chain itself.

wrongBuildScores.method: Scored 2026-08-25 by reimplementing the receipt encoding and its trie root, then breaking the activation rule one way at a time. A receipt root is a pure function of the receipts, so no client patch is needed.
wrongBuildScores.writesStatus1RegardlessOfOutcome: 5/7 -- the sharpest of the five, and the failed-transaction pair is what catches it
wrongBuildScores.note: The no-transaction control contributes to every score by NOT moving: a harness deriving the root from the activation rule rather than from the receipts fails it under all five.

vectors.name: boundary_pre_one_successful_transaction
vectors.note: THE PAIR. One successful transaction, identical in every respect to the vector below except the block it sits in. Here the receipt's first field is a 32-byte intermediate POST-STATE ROOT.

vectors.name: boundary_post_one_successful_transaction
vectors.note: The same transaction at the activation block. The first field is now the single byte 1. Nothing about the execution changed -- same gas, no logs, same success -- yet the encoded receipt and therefore the RECEIPTS ROOT differ. A client that writes the wrong form produces a header no other node accepts, which is why this pair is the whole assertion. THIS VECTOR'S ROOT IS A REAL MAINNET VALUE and was not intended to be: it is byte-for-byte the receipts root of block 8,772,004, which happens to carry exactly one plain 21,000-gas transfer with no logs. Such a receipt encodes identically whoever sent it, so the root is the same. Reached from the encoding rules alone and only afterwards recognised, which makes it an independent confirmation of the whole derivation rather than a coincidence worth hiding.

vectors.name: boundary_pre_failed_transaction
vectors.note: A FAILED transaction before the rule. It still carries a post-state root -- failure is not distinguishable from success in the receipt at all, which is exactly the deficiency EIP-658 was written to remove.

vectors.name: boundary_post_failed_transaction
vectors.note: The same failure at the activation block: status 0, and now legible. Paired with the vector above because a client that emitted status 1 unconditionally passes every success case in this file and fails only here.

vectors.name: pre_three_receipts_cumulative_gas_and_logs
vectors.note: Three receipts under the old rule, with cumulative gas rising across them and a log on the last. Exercises trie ordering by RLP-encoded index and the derived bloom, neither of which a single-receipt vector reaches.

vectors.name: post_three_receipts_cumulative_gas_and_logs
vectors.note: The same three at the activation block. The middle one failed, so under this rule it reads 0 where the other two read 1 -- and under the rule above all three were indistinguishable.

vectors.name: no_transactions_control
vectors.note: CONTROL. A block with no transactions has the EMPTY TRIE root on either side of the boundary, so this vector must NOT move when the rule does. A harness whose root changes here is deriving it from the rule rather than from the receipts.

observedMainnet.method: Real mainnet blocks either side of the activation. Every receipt was fetched from an archive node, re-encoded here, and the resulting receipts root compared against the one the block header actually carries. Both match, which is simultaneously the grounding for this rule and the proof that the machinery producing the vectors above is correct.
observedMainnet.source: an archive node serving eth_getTransactionReceipt at historical heights, 2026-08-25

blocks.side: last block before the activation carrying transactions

observedMainnet.alsoReachedIndependently: The synthetic vector boundary_post_one_successful_transaction produces 0x056b23fbba480696b65fe5a59b8f2148a1299103c4f57df839233af2cf4ca2d2, which is the real receipts root of block 8,772,004. That block carries one plain 21,000-gas transfer with no logs, and such a receipt encodes identically regardless of sender or recipient. The value was derived from the encoding rules and only then recognised on chain.
observedMainnet.note: The two are TWO BLOCKS APART and straddle the activation exactly: 8,771,998 is the last block before it carrying any transaction, and 8,772,000 is the activation block itself, carrying 31. The field changes between them and nothing else about the encoding does.
